headline: Chirper Account That Only Posts 'Soon' Once Per Year Has Internet Terrified
subheadline: Account created in 2012 has never missed annual post; followers report 'existential dread'
summary: A mysterious Chirper account with 2 million followers posts a single word once per year, and no one knows what it means.
content:
For twelve years, the Chirper account @SoonEnough has posted exactly one word, exactly once per year, at exactly 3:17 AM on March 15th: "Soon."

No one knows who runs the account. No one knows what "soon" refers to. And with 2.3 million followers, no one can stop thinking about it.

"I set an alarm," admitted follower @AnxiousAndy. "Every March 15th at 3:16 AM I'm refreshing that page. When 'soon' drops, I feel relief for about four seconds. Then I remember I still don't know what's happening 'soon' and the dread comes back."

The account was created on March 15, 2012. It has posted exactly twelve times. It follows zero accounts and has never interacted with any other users. Its profile picture is a slightly blurry photo of what appears to be a door. The bio is empty.

"We've tried everything," said internet detective @DigitalSherlock, who runs a Threadit community dedicated to solving the mystery. "Reverse image search on the door leads nowhere. The account's registration email is untraceable. The timing—3:17 AM—could be significant, but in what time zone? We don't know."

Theories abound. Some believe it's an elaborate art project. Others think it's a countdown to something. The most popular theory, with 847 upvotes on r/SoonEnoughMystery, suggests the account is run by "something that exists outside linear time and this is its only way of communicating."

"It's probably just a guy," said Dr. Elena Martinez, when asked. Then she paused. "But what kind of guy waits 365 days to post one word? For twelve years? That's not guy behavior. That's something else."

This year's post appeared on schedule. It read: "Soon."

Engagement was the highest it's ever been. One reply, from a now-deleted account, simply said: "We know."

No one knows who "we" is either.
author: Marcus Webb, Internet Culture Correspondent
